steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on fully unsupervised evaluation metrics for machine translation. It should motivate why new metrics are needed, sort existing metrics by the kind of supervision they use, explain what we aim for and how we get there, and end with our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Why evaluation metrics matter; problems with lexical overlap metrics
2. Trend towards supervised metrics and its downsides
3. Classification of existing metrics by supervision (TYPE-1/2/3)
4. Our goal: fully unsupervised metrics, two use cases
5. Approach: self-learning plus two dualities
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Why evaluation metrics matter
- essential for judging progress in NLG tasks (MT, summarization); identify state-of-the-art in a key NLP technology
- classical lexical overlap metrics: BLEU, ROUGE; widely disseminated
- difficulties judging quality of modern NLG systems -> need novel metrics correlating better with humans
- very active research area lately

2. Supervised metrics trend
- more and more supervised metrics
- BLEURT: human annotated datasets, 5k-150k pairs
- COMET models: regress on 12k-370k data points
- UniTE: pre-trains on 5m-10m parallel sentences, then fine-tunes on same data as COMET
- more data -> better metrics (in-domain), but risk of learning biases from data; limits applicability to domains / language pairs with supervision
- we go the opposite route: minimize supervision

3. Classification (cf. Table 1)
- TYPE-1: trained on human assessments (Direct-Assessment (DA), Post-Editing (PE) scores); compare outputs to human references or directly to source texts
- TYPE-2: no human assessments for training but need human references -> untrained, reference-based
- TYPE-3: untrained (unlike TYPE-1), reference-free (unlike TYPE-2); still rely on parallel data, which counts as supervision e.g. in the MT community

4. Our goal
- fully unsupervised metrics (for MT), no supervision of any form (cf. Table 1)
- under that constraint: maximally high quality = correlation with human assessments
- use case (a): sample efficiency -> wide applicability; overcome English-centricity of MT systems and metrics; low-resource languages (Nepali, Sinhala), low-resource pairs (Yoruba-German)
- use case (b): strong lower bounds for future work with (mild) supervision; push lower bounds for new TYPE-k metrics

5. Approach (cf. Figure 1)
- self-learning
- duality 1: metrics <-> NLG systems; metric as optimization criterion for a system; system generates pseudo references (a.o.) to improve a metric
- duality 2: metrics <-> parallel corpus mining; metric mines parallel data, data improves metric, e.g. remapping deficient embedding spaces

6. Contributions
- (i) effective unsupervised metrics via parallel corpus mining + MT system induction
- (ii) (a) efficient parallel corpus mining (overcome cubic runtime complexity); (b) unsupervised multilingual sentence embeddings from pseudo-parallel data
- (iii) pseudo-parallel data rectifies deficient vector spaces such as mBERT
- (iv) beat three state-of-the-art supervised metrics on four of five datasets

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Evaluation metrics are very important for judging progress in natural language generation (NLG) tasks like machine translation (MT) and summarization, because they tell us what the state-of-the-art is in a key NLP technology. Classical lexical overlap metrics like BLEU and ROUGE are widely used, but they have difficulties judging the quality of modern NLG systems, so we need new metrics that correlate better with humans. This has been a very active research area lately.

Recently more and more supervised metrics have been proposed. For example BLEURT trains on human annotated datasets with 5k-150k pairs, the COMET models regress on 12k-370k data points, and UniTE pre-trains on 5m-10m parallel sentences before it is fine-tuned on the same data as COMET. Training on more data of course leads to better metrics (measured on in-domain data), but it also increases the risk of learning biases from the data, and it limits the applicability to domains and language pairs where supervision is available. In this work we go the opposite way and try to use as little supervision as possible.

We classify the existing metrics according to the types of supervision they use (cf. Table 1). TYPE-1 metrics are trained on human assessments like Direct-Assessment (DA) or Post-Editing (PE) scores, and they compare the system outputs either to human references or directly to the source texts. TYPE-2 metrics do not use human assessments for training, but they still need human references, so they are untrained and reference-based. TYPE-3 metrics are untrained (unlike TYPE-1) and reference-free (unlike TYPE-2), so they do not use supervision like TYPE-1 or 2. But to work well they still rely on parallel data, and parallel data is considered a form of supervision, for example in the MT community.

4. Our goal
- fully unsupervised metrics (for MT), no supervision of any form (cf. Table 1)
- under that constraint: maximally high quality = correlation with human assessments
- use case (a): sample efficiency -> wide applicability; overcome English-centricity of MT systems and metrics; low-resource languages (Nepali, Sinhala), low-resource pairs (Yoruba-German)
- use case (b): strong lower bounds for future work with (mild) supervision; push lower bounds for new TYPE-k metrics

5. Approach (cf. Figure 1)
- self-learning
- duality 1: metrics <-> NLG systems; metric as optimization criterion for a system; system generates pseudo references (a.o.) to improve a metric
- duality 2: metrics <-> parallel corpus mining; metric mines parallel data, data improves metric, e.g. remapping deficient embedding spaces

6. Contributions
- (i) effective unsupervised metrics via parallel corpus mining + MT system induction
- (ii) (a) efficient parallel corpus mining (overcome cubic runtime complexity); (b) unsupervised multilingual sentence embeddings from pseudo-parallel data
- (iii) pseudo-parallel data rectifies deficient vector spaces such as mBERT
- (iv) beat three state-of-the-art supervised metrics on four of five datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Evaluation metrics are very important for judging progress in natural language generation (NLG) tasks like machine translation (MT) and summarization, because they tell us what the state-of-the-art is in a key NLP technology. Classical lexical overlap metrics like BLEU and ROUGE are widely used, but they have difficulties judging the quality of modern NLG systems, so we need new metrics that correlate better with humans. This has been a very active research area lately.

Recently more and more supervised metrics have been proposed. For example BLEURT trains on human annotated datasets with 5k-150k pairs, the COMET models regress on 12k-370k data points, and UniTE pre-trains on 5m-10m parallel sentences before it is fine-tuned on the same data as COMET. Training on more data of course leads to better metrics (measured on in-domain data), but it also increases the risk of learning biases from the data, and it limits the applicability to domains and language pairs where supervision is available. In this work we go the opposite way and try to use as little supervision as possible.

We classify the existing metrics according to the types of supervision they use (cf. Table 1). TYPE-1 metrics are trained on human assessments like Direct-Assessment (DA) or Post-Editing (PE) scores, and they compare the system outputs either to human references or directly to the source texts. TYPE-2 metrics do not use human assessments for training, but they still need human references, so they are untrained and reference-based. TYPE-3 metrics are untrained (unlike TYPE-1) and reference-free (unlike TYPE-2), so they do not use supervision like TYPE-1 or 2. But to work well they still rely on parallel data, and parallel data is considered a form of supervision, for example in the MT community.

We instead aim for fully unsupervised evaluation metrics (for MT), which do not use any form of supervision at all (cf. Table 1). Also, under the constraint that no supervision is allowed, our metrics should have as high quality as possible, i.e. correlation with human assessments. We have two use cases in mind. (a) This kind of sample efficiency is needed for the metrics to be widely applicable. It is especially important if we want to overcome the current English-centricity of MT systems and evaluation metrics and also cover low-resource languages like Nepali or Sinhala and low-resource pairs like Yoruba-German. (b) Our fully unsupervised metrics should be strong lower bounds for any future work that uses (mild) forms of supervision to induce metrics, so we want to push the lower bounds for new TYPE-k metrics.

To do this we use self-learning, and in particular we use the following dualities to make our metrics as effective as possible, cf. Figure 1: 1. Evaluation metrics and NLG systems are closely related. For example a metric can be used as an optimization criterion for an NLG system, and the other way around a system can generate pseudo references (a.o.) that can be used to improve a metric. 2. Evaluation metrics and parallel corpus mining are closely related. For example a metric can be used to mine parallel data, and this data can then be used to improve the metric, e.g. by remapping deficient embedding spaces.

Our contributions are: (i) we show that we can get effective unsupervised evaluation metrics by exploiting the relationships with parallel corpus mining approaches and MT system induction; (ii) for this we explore ways to (a) make parallel corpus mining efficient (e.g. overcome cubic runtime complexity) and (b) induce unsupervised multilingual sentence embeddings from pseudo-parallel data; (iii) we show that pseudo-parallel data can fix deficient vector spaces like mBERT; (iv) we show that our metrics beat three state-of-the-art supervised metrics on four of five datasets we evaluate on.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Evaluation metrics are essential for judging progress in natural language generation (NLG) tasks such as machine translation (MT) and summarization, since they identify the state-of-the-art in a key NLP technology. Despite being widely used, classical lexical overlap metrics like BLEU [1] and ROUGE [2] have difficulties judging the quality of modern NLG systems [3,4], which makes novel metrics that correlate better with humans necessary. Lately, this has been a very active research area [5,6,7,8,9].

Recently, more and more supervised metrics have been proposed. E.g., BLEURT [10] trains on human annotated datasets ranging from 5k-150k pairs, the COMET [11] models regress on 12k-370k data points and UniTE [12], before fine-tuning on the same data as COMET, pre-trains on 5m-10m parallel sentences. Of course, training on larger amounts of data leads to better metrics (measured on in-domain data), but it also increases the risk of learning biases from the data [13] and limits the applicability to domains and language pairs where supervision is available. Here, we go the opposite route and try to minimize the amount of supervision as much as possible.

We classify existing metrics by the different types of supervision they use as follows (cf. Table 1). TYPE-1 metrics are trained on human assessments such as Direct-Assessment (DA) or Post-Editing (PE) scores, and compare system outputs either to human references [10,11] or directly to source texts [14]. TYPE-2 metrics, by comparison, do not use human assessments for training but still require human references, i.e., they are untrained and reference-based [9,6,5]. Finally, TYPE-3 metrics are untrained (unlike TYPE-1) and reference-free (unlike TYPE-2), i.e., they do not use supervision as in TYPE-1 or 2. However, to work well, they still rely on parallel data [15,16], which is considered a form of supervision, e.g., in the MT community [17,18].

In contrast, we aim for fully unsupervised evaluation metrics (for MT) that do not use any form of supervision (cf. Table 1). In addition, subject to the constraint that no supervision is allowed, our metrics should be of maximally high quality, i.e., correlation with human assessments. We have two use cases in mind: (a) Such sample efficiency is a prerequisite for the wide applicability of the metrics. This is especially important if we want to overcome the current English-centricity [19] of MT systems and evaluation metrics and also cover low-resource languages like Nepali or Sinhala [20] and low-resource pairs like Yoruba-German. (b) Our fully unsupervised evaluation metrics should serve as strong lower bounds for any future work that uses (mild) forms of supervision for metric induction, i.e., we want to push the lower bounds for newly developed TYPE-k metrics.

To achieve these goals, we employ self-learning [21,22] and, in particular, leverage the following dualities to make our metrics maximally effective, cf. Figure 1: 1. Evaluation metrics and NLG systems are closely related; e.g., a metric can be an optimization criterion for an NLG system [23], and conversely a system can generate pseudo references (a.o.) from which a metric can be improved. 2. Evaluation metrics and parallel corpus mining [24] are closely related; e.g., a metric can be used to mine parallel data, which in turn can be used to improve the metric [15], e.g., by remapping deficient embedding spaces.

Our contributions are: (i) We show that effective unsupervised evaluation metrics can be obtained by exploiting the relationships with parallel corpus mining approaches and MT system induction; (ii) to do so, we explore ways to (a) make parallel corpus mining efficient (e.g., overcome cubic runtime complexity) and (b) induce unsupervised multilingual sentence embeddings from pseudo-parallel data; (iii) we show that pseudo-parallel data can rectify deficient vector spaces such as mBERT; (iv) we show that our metrics beat three state-of-the-art supervised metrics on four of the five datasets we evaluate on.
